rulings.rationale: Rule 6 skips the legislative internship; the remaining items (assistant manager of a small program, press assistant, startup communications) are uniformly junior assistant-grade non-manual roles. 'Assistant manager' is an assistant grade, not a manager, so II's 'manager without evidence of scale' clause does not attach; routine non-manual fits the whole string.
rulings.note: Rubric does not address 'assistant'-prefixed titles; rule 1's manager clause pulled coder A toward II.

rulings.rationale: Rule 8: consultant with named field codes on the field. The field is farm/agri-environmental advisory (REPS planning), which is adviser work, not chartered agronomy: farming advisers are associate professionals, II.
rulings.note: Rubric ambiguity: rule 8's ISCO crosswalk splits by ISCO version (ISCO-88 farming advisers = associate professional II; ISCO-08 2132 = professional I). The string did not cause the split; the crosswalk did.

rulings.rationale: Rule 2's professional carve-out governs: the consultancy company IS the professional practice, so an IT/computing consultant on own account codes on the profession, and computing professionals are I (rule 8). The trucking-company example covers non-professional proprietorship, which this is not.

Shop steward is a lay union office held alongside an unstated occupation; it implies employee status but not sector or skill level (could be VIIab, V/VI, or even III in a white-collar union). Rule 7: unknown rather than a guess.
Rule 5: first-listed is agricultural consultant; coded identically to occ2_4262 as farm advisory work, II. Barrister is second-listed and recorded elsewhere, not coded.
rulings.note: Same rule-8 crosswalk ambiguity as occ2_4262 (agronomist I vs farming adviser II); ruled II for consistency with occ2_4262.

rulings.rationale: 'Activist with Friends of the Earth' states no employment relation; twenty years of activism is fully consistent with a voluntary avocation alongside an unstated occupation. Rule 7: coding it as paid NGO campaigner (II) is an assumption the string does not support.

First-listed is 'laboratory worker', which spans routine operative (VIIab), routine assistant (III) and technician (V/VI); nothing in the string selects among them. Rule 7 prefers a missing code to a silent wrong one.

Chairperson of a football club is characteristically a non-executive or voluntary board position, not an employment relation; the underlying occupation is unstated. Rule 7 applies; rule 1 presupposes an occupational headship, which this string does not establish.

'Healthcare worker' spans nurse (II), care assistant (III) and aide (VIIab); professional grades would ordinarily be named, but that inference cannot carry a class assignment on its own. Rule 7: unknown.

The string is exhausted by affiliation to a political-military movement; no substantive occupation is stated. Coded none-political in the spirit of rule 6: the recorded identity is political, not occupational.
rulings.note: Rubric gap: rule 6 enumerates elected and party roles but not paramilitary membership, which caused the none-political/unknown split.

rulings.rationale: Rule 5 fixes coding on the first-listed item, 'Stena Line employee', which gives no role or grade (seaman to manager all possible) — rule 7 makes that unknown. The rental sideline is second-listed and cannot be promoted over it.

Green Party candidacy is political (rule 6) and 'environmental activist', paired with the candidacy, reads as part of the same political persona rather than a substantive occupation; no employment relation is stated anywhere, so the string is exhausted by political items.
rulings.note: Rubric gap: 'activist' is classified by neither rule 6 nor the class schema; ruled none-political here (candidacy anchors the string as political) versus unknown for occ2_4337 (no political item present).

rulings.rationale: One law-enforcement career; rule 5's worked example ('police officer, rising to Superintendent') directs coding at the stated level, not the entry grade. County sheriff is head of the agency, a supervisory/managerial grade of the career: II.
rulings.note: Rubric tension: rule 6 (elected office) versus rule 5 (career at stated level) pull against each other for elected sheriffs; rule 5's explicit police example was taken as controlling.

rulings.rationale: Same single policing career as occ2_4522, coded at its stated senior level (sheriff, agency head) per rule 5: II. Ruled identically to occ2_4522 for consistency.
rulings.note: Same rule 5 versus rule 6 tension over elected sheriffs as occ2_4522.

rulings.rationale: Party official is political (rule 6). State labor commissioner is elected office in some US states and an appointed administrative headship in others; the string does not say which, so it underdetermines none-political versus I. Rule 7: unknown.

Grant MacEwan was a community college through most of the stated tenure; a program chair is a college-level teacher with managerial duty over a program, not head of the institution — semi-professional with supervisory responsibility, II. The rubric places professors in I but teachers and technicians-with-supervision in II; college instruction sits with the latter.

One education career (teacher, then head of a private boarding school), coded at its stated level per rule 5. A school headship is lower administration of a small organisation under rule 1 — head teachers/principals map to II, and Athol Murray is not evidently a large organisation: II.

Rule 6: campaign work is political, and it is the only role stated; attending law school is not an occupation, and being a classmate of a politician is nothing at all. The political item exhausts the string's occupational content, which is what none-political denotes; unknown would misreport a string whose content is stated but political.
Rule 1's worked rule is explicit: head of the firm is I; functional directors are II. Head of exploration is a functional division head within Canadian Fina, not head of the firm: II.
rulings.note: Rubric tension caused the split: rule 1's functional-director clause (II) collides with I's 'managers of large organisations' for senior functional executives of large firms. The more specific worked rule was applied.

rulings.rationale: Rule 6 skips MLA and cabinet minister; the substantive item is founder of a private school. Rule 2: ownership codes IVab unless the firm is clearly large, and the string itself states no scale.
rulings.note: Rubric ambiguity: the split turns on whether external knowledge of Webber Academy's size is admissible; the rubric says to code the organisation implied but is silent on outside knowledge. Coded from the string.

rulings.rationale: 'Steel metal worker' read as steelworker requires no emendation, while the craft reading requires correcting it to 'sheet metal worker'; in a Nova Scotia record the steel-plant process worker (Sydney Steel) is the modal referent. VIIab, but only just — the craft reading remains live, hence low confidence.

Bare 'business person' states neither employment relation (owner, executive, self-employed) nor scale. The rubric has a modal-case rule for 'farmer' (rule 3) but deliberately none for 'businessman', so rule 7 governs: unknown rather than the IVab guess.

'A director of' a firm is an unspecified directorship, not stated headship: rule 1's worked rule sends heads of firms to I but unspecified directors/managers to II. Deco Labels is not evidently large from the string, and an ownership (IVab) reading is also unstated.
rulings.note: Rubric gap: rule 1 grades managing directors and functional directors but not a bare board directorship of a private family firm, which is what split the coders.

rulings.rationale: String is a name plus peerage; no occupation or landholding stated. Inferring 'large landed proprietor' from a title is an assumption the string does not support (rule 7: a wrong code is worse than a missing one).
rulings.note: Rubric ambiguity: the rubric is silent on hereditary titles/peerages; this same split recurs at occ2_1851 and occ2_1945 in both directions, so the rubric, not the strings, caused it. A peerage rule should be added.

rulings.rationale: Rule 6 skips the cabinet-minister item; 'newspaper editor' with no scale or title-of-paper evidence codes with journalists in II — rule 1's worked rule sends unspecified functional/managerial roles to II, and the rubric explicitly lists journalist in II. Must match occ2_2119 (same person).
Hereditary earldom only; no occupation or landholding stated. Same ruling as occ2_1826/occ2_1945 for consistency.
rulings.note: Rubric ambiguity: no rule for peerages (see occ2_1826).

rulings.rationale: First-listed 'IT worker' spans helpdesk (III) to professional (I) (rule 4 analogue, rule 7); the slash may even denote a single self-employed role (IVab). The string underdetermines among three classes.

General Secretary is head of the NCCL, a national organisation not evidently tiny from the string; rule 1's worked rule defaults heads of actual organisations to I. The press-secretary item is political staff (rule 6) and skipped.
rulings.note: Rubric ambiguity, mild: rule 1 speaks of 'firms'; heads of national NGOs/pressure groups sit between its 'head of firm → I' default and its 'two-person non-profit → II' example.

rulings.rationale: 'Treasury official' determinately connotes administrative-grade civil service (service class), but grade is unstated; by rule 1's default-down principle (unspecified managers/administrators → lower service) codes II. Policy Unit item is political staff (rule 6).
rulings.note: Rubric ambiguity: rule 3 gives a modal default for 'farmer' but the rubric gives none for civil servants/officials; the I-vs-II split recurs across occ2_1917/1941 in both directions.

rulings.rationale: 'Colonial civil servant' in a UK parental record connotes the expatriate administrative service — determinately service class — but grade is unstated, so rule 1's default-down sends it to II rather than I.
rulings.note: Rubric ambiguity: no grade default for civil servants (see occ2_1917).

rulings.rationale: Hereditary marquessate only; no occupation or landholding stated (rule 7). Same string family as occ2_1826 (same person) — must match its ruling.
rulings.note: Rubric ambiguity: no rule for peerages (see occ2_1826).

rulings.rationale: 'Director, Barclays' is an unspecified director, not stated to be head of the firm — in banking the title spans main board to mid-rank; rule 1's worked rule sends unspecified/functional directors to II. Main-board reading would need evidence the string lacks.
'Finance director' is precisely a functional director, which rule 1 assigns to II regardless of firm size; subsidiary scale does not override the explicit functional-director clause.

First-listed 'bank risk manager' carries the title manager, and rule 1 assigns functional managers without evidence of scale to II; rule 8's finance-professional clause applies where the rubric is silent, but rule 1 speaks directly to manager titles.
rulings.note: Rubric ambiguity: rule 1 (unspecified manager → II) and rule 8 (finance professional → I) genuinely collide on professionalised manager titles like risk manager; the rubric should state which wins.

rulings.rationale: First-listed 'local government officer' is a generic UK term spanning clerical (III) through professional/administrative (II) to chief officer (I); grade unstated (rule 7). Ruled unknown even though neither coder chose it — the string underdetermines between their two defensible readings.
rulings.note: Rubric ambiguity: no modal/default rule for bare UK 'officer' grades; the same term splits four ways across occ2_1981/2115/2235/2347.

rulings.rationale: Rule 8 governs where the rubric is silent: advertising/marketing and communications professionals are ISCO business professionals, mapping to I. The rubric's II list names journalist but not advertising, so the crosswalk clause decides.
Commissioned officer is determinately service class, but rank is unstated; consistent default-down (as with unspecified administrators, rule 1) codes II. Same ruling applied to occ2_2176/2265/2318.
rulings.note: Rubric ambiguity: no rule for military commissioned ranks; this identical split recurs four times in both directions, proving the rubric caused it.

rulings.rationale: First-listed 'Unilever employee' is wholly role-indeterminate (rule 7), and rule 5 forbids skipping to the second-listed administrator; falling through to codeable later items would bias the distribution.
rulings.note: Rubric gap: rules 5 and 7 do not say what to do when the first-listed item is uncodeable; B's fall-through and A's unknown are both rubric-consistent (also at occ2_2303/2401/2432).

rulings.rationale: 'Local government officer' grade unstated spans III to I; 'former miner' is a prior occupation, not the principal one (rule 5). Consistent with occ2_1981/2235/2347.
rulings.note: Rubric ambiguity: no default rule for bare council-officer grades (see occ2_1981).

rulings.rationale: Same person and same string content as occ2_1842; rule 6 skips the ministerial item and the unspecified newspaper editor codes II with journalists. Rulings must match across the pair.

First-listed Grenadier Guardsman is an army other-rank in a combat infantry role; the rubric's V/VI other-ranks clause deliberately names only police and fire, and the standard crosswalk sends armed-forces other ranks to VIIab.
rulings.note: Rubric ambiguity: the omission of military other ranks from the V/VI clause is what split the coders; the rubric should state the military rule explicitly.

rulings.rationale: A Wren's trade is unstated and WRNS trades genuinely spanned clerical/signals (III) through domestic and mechanical work (VIIab); unlike an infantry Guardsman there is no determinate role, so rule 7 applies.
rulings.note: Rubric ambiguity: no rule for military service, and none for trade-unspecified enlisted service (see occ2_2120).

rulings.rationale: Deputy chief executive of the NHS Confederation, a national body — the string itself supplies scale evidence, and a deputy chief executive of a national organisation is a higher administrator (rule 1), not a functional or unspecified manager.
First-listed British Army officer, rank unstated: commissioned officer defaults down to II (see occ2_2025); rule 5 keeps the officer item over pharmacist.
rulings.note: Rubric ambiguity: no military-rank rule (see occ2_2025).

rulings.rationale: 'Law lecturer and barrister': law lecturing is modally a higher-education teaching post (crosswalk: HE teaching professionals → I), and the paired barrister career corroborates the professional reading; assumption stated per medium confidence.
rulings.note: Rubric ambiguity: the rubric places professor in I and teacher in II but leaves 'lecturer' unplaced; this also drove the occ2_2472 split.

rulings.rationale: Olympic football was amateur-era; the string states athletic status, not an employment relation, and no occupation is given (rule 7). Coding II via the sportsperson crosswalk requires assuming a professional career the string contradicts.

Founded and ran his own lobbying firm: own-account proprietor (rule 2). The professional-exception in rule 2 covers credentialled (semi-)professions practised on own account; lobbying is not one, so ownership governs.

Au pair is childcare/personal-service work, not cleaning; the rubric's III explicitly includes 'service' (IIIb collapsed in), and the crosswalk puts childcare workers with routine service rather than with cleaners in VIIab.
'District council officer', grade unstated, spans clerical to chief officer; consistent with occ2_1981/2115/2347 (rule 7).
rulings.note: Rubric ambiguity: no default rule for bare council-officer grades (see occ2_1981).

rulings.rationale: A headteacher is head of an actual organisation, not evidently tiny (rule 1 default), and the crosswalk maps school heads to education managers in I; the II reading requires reading the school as small without evidence.
Army officer, rank unstated: commissioned officer defaults down to II, consistent with occ2_2025/2176/2318.
rulings.note: Rubric ambiguity: no military-rank rule (see occ2_2025).

rulings.rationale: Principal occupation is 'civil servant', grade unstated (spans III to I, rule 7); 'formerly electrician' is an explicitly prior occupation, and coding it would misstate the principal role that rule 5 selects.
rulings.note: Rubric gap: no rule for an uncodeable principal item (see occ2_2087), and no grade default for bare 'civil servant'.

rulings.rationale: Army officer, rank unstated: commissioned officer defaults down to II, consistent with occ2_2025/2176/2265.
rulings.note: Rubric ambiguity: no military-rank rule (see occ2_2025).

rulings.rationale: First-listed 'local government officer, Liverpool Corporation' carries no grade; the term spans III to I (rule 7), and rule 5 bars falling through to the lecturer item. Consistent with occ2_1981/2115/2235.
rulings.note: Rubric ambiguity: no default rule for bare council-officer grades (see occ2_1981).

rulings.rationale: UK usage distinguishes 'assistant librarian' (junior qualified librarian, semi-professional → II) from 'library assistant' (clerical → III); the string says the former, so B's crosswalk reading conflates two distinct titles.

Bare 'civil servant' spans clerk (III) to higher administrator (I); the rubric provides a modal default only for farmers (rule 3), so coding the modal clerical grade is a guess the rubric does not license (rule 7).
rulings.note: Rubric ambiguity: no modal/default rule for bare 'civil servant'; drove splits at occ2_2366/2303/2401/2432.

rulings.rationale: Chapel minister is clergy, listed directly in II; B's coding is missing, not a substantive disagreement.

First-listed 'civil servant, Ministry of Civil Aviation' carries no grade (III to I span); rule 5 selects it as principal and does not permit skipping to the news-editor item, so the ruling is unknown rather than II. Consistent with occ2_2087/2303/2432.
rulings.note: Rubric gap: no rule for an uncodeable first-listed item (see occ2_2087).

rulings.rationale: CND chairmanship is political-campaign leadership and exhausts the string; rule 6's principle — a political role is not a class origin — fits better than unknown, since the string is informative about what the role was.
rulings.note: Rubric ambiguity: rule 6 enumerates elected and party roles only; movement/campaign leadership is unlisted, which caused the split.

rulings.rationale: 'Technical officer' at ICI was historically a graduate-scientist grade, and the subsequent econometrics-researcher item corroborates the graduate professional-track reading over bench technician; higher-grade technician/associate professional codes II.

First-listed founder/director of Policy Exchange is head of an actual national organisation, not evidently tiny (rule 1), and the second item (firm chief executive) corroborates the higher-service reading.

'Assistant lecturer' is an explicitly junior higher-education teaching grade at a polytechnic; the rubric places professor in I and teacher in II, and the junior grade plus non-university institution place this at II, unlike the unmarked law lecturer at occ2_2199.
rulings.note: Rubric ambiguity: 'lecturer' is unplaced between professor (I) and teacher (II) — see occ2_2199.

rulings.rationale: Bare 'businessman' carries no class information (rule 7), so it cannot anchor rule 5; the codable item is sports executive of the Edmonton Oilers. He is an executive, not stated head or owner of the club, and rule 1 puts functional/unspecified executives in II regardless of organisation size.
rulings.note: Rubric gap contributed: rule 5 does not say what to do when the first-listed item ('businessman') is substantive but uninformative. I adopted: skip to the first codable occupation.

rulings.rationale: Rule 8: the standard ISCO-EGP crosswalk places mail carriers and sorting clerks with clerks, i.e. routine non-manual III. Union presidency is not an occupation. A's semi-skilled reading is defensible but the rubric explicitly defers to the crosswalk where silent.

Chalkwell Motor Co. is an evidently small local firm, so I is excluded; rule 2 requires stated ownership to move someone to IVab, and none is stated — 'Director' alone in a UK Ltd does not establish proprietorship. Rule 1's worked rule for directors of tiny organisations gives II.

General secretary is the head of War on Want, an actual national organisation. Rule 1's stated default is head-of-firm = I *unless evidently tiny*; a national charity is not evidently tiny. A inverted the default (requiring evidence of largeness), which the rubric does not ask for.

An international account manager handling corporate telecom accounts is a commercial-sales associate professional, not counter sales (III's exemplar is 'sales assistant'); rule 8's crosswalk places technical/commercial sales representatives and finance-sales associates in II, and rule 1 puts unspecified 'manager' titles in II.

Rule 5 first-listed is the advice worker. Rule 8: UK advice workers crosswalk to social-work/welfare associate professionals (ISCO 3460) → II rather than routine service. Low confidence — the routine-service reading is not unreasonable, but the crosswalk tips II.

Rule 5 makes 'publisher' the first-listed occupation, and 'publisher' spans I (head of a publishing house), IVab (small-press proprietor) and II; the string gives no scale, ownership or employer. Anchoring on 'journalist' evades rule 5, and defaulting the publisher to I guesses. Rule 7: unknown.

Rule 7's paradigm case: NGO employment ('worked with', 'worked for') with no stated role or level — could be an administrator, a programme professional or support staff. B's II is an assumption, not a reading of the string.

The string is explicitly chronological (dated 1965-1970 first), so rule 5's premise — that sources lead with the principal or most recent role — fails; the principal career is the solicitor partnership. Solicitor codes I on the profession (rule 2: partnership does not displace the professional coding). Either way the outcome is service-class: RN officer also crosswalks to I.
rulings.note: Rubric ambiguity: rule 5 assumes principal-first ordering and gives no instruction for demonstrably chronological, dated strings. This caused the split.

rulings.rationale: Industry labels plus 'positions at' four firms, with no role or level — structurally identical to rule 7's 'senior positions in the oil and gas industry' example. The string never says 'consultant' as his occupation, so rule 8's named-field-consultant clause does not attach. Unknown.

The source itself says 'unknown ... no pre-political career described'. This is missing data, not evidence that politics exhausted his working life — municipal politicians typically have prior day jobs the source simply omitted. none-political should mark career politicians, not absent records; rule 7 governs.
rulings.note: Rubric ambiguity: rules 6 and 7 collide when the only content is political but the source disclaims completeness. The rubric does not say which wins; I ruled that an explicit 'no career described' marker is missing data (rule 7), not an exhaustively-political record (rule 6).

rulings.rationale: Rule 4 says use context, and there is strong context: NUM membership and presidency. Chartered mining engineers were colliery management and belonged to management unions (BACM), not the NUM; an NUM president rose from the workforce, so 'mining engineer' here reads as colliery engineer/craftsman → V/VI. B's unknown ignores usable context that rule 4 directs us to use.

'Shop worker and manager' with no second employer reads as one retail career whose stated terminal grade is manager; rule 5's carve-out says grade progressions within one career code at the stated level, and rule 1 codes an unspecified manager as II.
rulings.note: Rubric ambiguity contributed: rule 5's within-career carve-out gives 'rising to' as its marker, and the rubric does not say whether an unmarked 'worker and manager' pairing counts as one career or two listed occupations.

rulings.rationale: 'Finance' is an industry, not an occupation, and Harvard Business School is a credential, not a role; rule 7 forbids inferring grade from sector plus plausibility. B's I converts an educational credential into an occupational relation the string never states.

Corporate pensions account manager: a finance-sales/finance-associate role with an unspecified 'manager' title and no staff or organisational scale — II under rule 1 and the rule 8 crosswalk for finance associate professionals. Coded consistently with occ2_3423.

The bar qualification was explicitly never practised, so it codes nothing. Everything then hangs on 'researcher': if political (the likely Tory-career reading, given Central Office follows) the string is exhausted by politics → none-political; if substantive it is II-ish. The string does not say which. Both coders' answers are defensible and the string underdetermines the class → unknown.

Ministry employment and 'environmental policy work' name an employer and activities but no gradeable role or employment relation — a ministry employee spans clerk to senior diplomat. Rule 7: code unknown rather than assume the professional track from a fellowship.

First-listed 'businessman' is uninformative (rule 7); the fallback occupation, loss-prevention officer, itself sits ambiguously across III and VIIab in standard crosswalks (retail security/protective services are not the rubric's police/fire V/VI exemplar). With both items unresolvable the string underdetermines the class.

Rule 8: the rubric is silent on the military, and standard ISCO-08-to-EGP crosswalks map commissioned armed-forces officers (0110) to I, NCOs to V/VI, other ranks to VIIab; the crosswalk does not grade within the commissioned ranks, so Captain does not demote to II.
rulings.note: Rubric ambiguity: the rubric gives no rank threshold for officers, and the crosswalk's officer/NCO cut is coarser than the I/II distinction B wanted to draw. This gap caused the split; the crosswalk default decides.

rulings.rationale: President of the Saint John Sea Dogs is head of an actual firm; rule 1's default is I unless the organisation is evidently tiny, and a QMJHL franchise is a real business, not evidently tiny. A applied the inverted test (demanding evidence of largeness). Ruled consistently with occ2_3417.

Rule 6 sets aside chief-of-staff and riding-organizer items; the substantive occupation is government policy analyst. Rule 8: policy/public-administration professionals (ISCO 2422/2470) crosswalk to I, like the business professionals the rubric names. B's II is defensible but the crosswalk the rubric defers to gives I.
Bare 'businessman' is uninformative and cannot be read as small proprietor without guessing (rule 7); the first codable occupation is firefighter, a rubric exemplar of V/VI (fire other-ranks).
rulings.note: Rubric gap: rule 5 does not address uncodable generic first items. Skipping to the first codable occupation (as in occ2_3378, occ2_4077) rather than ruling the whole string unknown is my adopted convention.

rulings.rationale: 'Financial processing analyst' and 'revenue and costing analyst' sit exactly on the II/III boundary — accounting associate professional versus transaction-processing clerical — and the string gives nothing to resolve it. Both coders were at low confidence on opposite sides; that is the coin-flip rule 7 exists to prevent.
Rule 8: standard crosswalks map commissioned armed-forces officers to I; 'British Army officer' states commissioned status and nothing lower. Ruled consistently with occ2_3682.
rulings.note: Same rubric gap as occ2_3682: no rank guidance for the military; crosswalk default decides.

rulings.rationale: Special adviser is political (rule 6); the substantive role is director (head) of Policy Exchange, an actual and prominent national think-tank, not evidently tiny → I under rule 1's default. Consistent with occ2_3417 and occ2_3687.

'Policy advisor, European Parliament' does not say whether the employer was a political group (analogous to rule 6's caucus staff → none-political) or the Parliament's secretariat (a civil-service II). No group or party is named. Both readings are defensible and the string underdetermines which side of the rule 6 line the job falls on.

Rule 1 licenses coding 'the organisation implied' by a named entity, and Directed Electronics is a large, publicly-traded consumer-electronics firm — this is Issa's Viper alarm company, hundreds of employees. Rule 2's own exception applies: an owner of a clearly large firm is a large proprietor, I, not IVab.

An Assistant Secretary in a US state government is a senior appointed official heading a policy division of a large administration — the 'higher administrators and officials' of class I (the equivalent UK Assistant Secretary grade is classically coded higher service). A's sub-head-therefore-lower reading imports rule 1's firm logic into a government hierarchy where the grade itself is senior.

Rule 4: 'engineer' is ambiguous in North American records and the only context is 'and consultant', which is suggestive of professional practice but establishes nothing — and rule 8's consultant clause is circular here since the only field named is the ambiguous 'engineer'. Rule 4's explicit instruction for absent context is unknown, not the more flattering guess.

Homemaking carries no EGP code, and 'a career in education' names a sector, not a role — teacher (II), assistant (III) and administrator all fit. Rule 7: the teaching assumption is plausible but unstated; code unknown.

The concrete occupation is founder-proprietor of his own small research firm — rule 2's default is IVab. The profession carve-out in rule 2 covers credentialled professions and the rubric's listed semi-professions; running a small advertising/market-research agency is agency proprietorship, not solo professional practice, and the firm is not clearly large.

First-listed 'health dept. worker' states no role and is uncodable; the first codable occupation is driver for the mayor — a chauffeur, and 'driver' is a rubric exemplar of VIIab. Legislative aide is political (rule 6).
rulings.note: Same rubric gap as occ2_3703: no instruction for uncodable first items; skipping to the first codable occupation rather than ruling unknown is the adopted convention.

rulings.rationale: 'Businesswoman and educator' is a summary label resolved by the concrete roles that follow: manager of international programs at a polytechnic (unspecified manager, rule 1 → II) and community-college instructor (II). Both codable readings agree on II; no ownership is stated to support IVab.

'Senior corporate management' names no organisation, so rule 1's scale requirement for I is unmet — unspecified managers are II. A's I requires assuming a large organisation the string never provides. (The founder item is second-listed; rule 5 keeps the management career.)

Two distinct listed occupations, hotel manager and restaurateur; rule 5 selects the first-listed, and an unspecified hotel manager is II under rule 1. Reading the pair as one proprietorship (so the 'manager' owns the hotel) is an inference the string does not state, and rule 2 requires stated ownership for IVab.

'Partner' states co-ownership, and rule 2 moves owners to IVab, not up the service classes; the Benjamin Group is not evidently large and no credentialled profession is named that would trigger rule 2's practice carve-out. The VP title describes his function within a firm he co-owns.

Rule 5 first-listed: Conestoga College professor. A Canadian community college is non-university post-secondary vocational education; the crosswalk places vocational/further-education teachers (ISCO 2320) in II, not university teachers (2310, I). B's FE-lecturer assimilation is the standard mapping.

Rule 5 first-listed: Mary Kay cosmetics saleswoman. Mary Kay sellers are own-account direct-sales consultants paid on commission, and 'commission agents' are an explicit IVab exemplar in the rubric; the 'for Mary Kay' phrasing describes the brand relationship, not an employment contract.

Rule 8's own sentence decides this boundary: 'business, finance and computing professionals are I', and financial/investment advisers crosswalk to finance professionals (ISCO 2412). B's associate-professional demotion is defensible but the rubric's explicit finance-professional clause tips I.

'Worked at his family law firm' states an employer, not a role — attorney, office manager and clerk all fit, and the string never says he was a lawyer. Rule 7: the attorney reading is plausible but not established, and a silently wrong I is worse than a missing value.

Chief executive = head of an autonomous national membership organisation (LGiU); string gives no evidence it is tiny, so rule 1's default (head of an actual organisation is I unless evidently tiny) applies.
rulings.note: Rubric-caused split: rule 1 places the burden on 'evidently tiny', but gives no guidance for small policy/think-tank organisations whose scale the string never states.

rulings.rationale: Nurse director is a functional director within a hospital, not head of the organisation; rule 1's worked rule puts functional directors in II, and the nursing career base is also II.
MD of a family firm is a proprietor-director; rule 2 sends ownership to IVab unless the firm is clearly large, and 'family leather firm' gives no evidence of scale.

First-listed occupation is Royal Navy officer (rule 5). Rank unstated; without evidence of senior rank, coding the lower service class avoids inflation, consistent with rule 1's scale-not-title principle.
rulings.note: Rubric-caused split: the schema lists only police/fire other-ranks (V/VI) and is silent on commissioned officers; both I and II crosswalk conventions exist.

rulings.rationale: Academic economist lecturing at multiple universities = higher-education teaching professional, crosswalks to I.
'Lay' marks a part-time public appointment explicitly held by a non-professional; it is a role, not an occupation, and the underlying occupation is not stated (rule 7).

Shipbroker employed at two named firms (Braemar ACM, Poten & Partners) — an employee, not own-account. IVab is petty bourgeoisie and requires own-account status; employed finance/commercial broker codes as associate professional II.
rulings.note: Rubric-caused split: IVab's list names 'brokers' without the own-account qualifier that defines the class.

rulings.rationale: 'Civil servant (Whitehall)' states no grade; the category spans clerical (III) through administrative class (I). Both coders' service-class readings are assumptions the string does not support, so unknown per rule 7.
'Senior executive' is a senior manager but not head of the firm, and scale is not evidently large; rule 1's worked rule codes non-head managers II.

First-listed substantive occupation is surveyor (rule 5); rule 2 codes a partner practising a profession on the profession, not the proprietorship, and UK surveyors in named professional partnerships are modally chartered professionals (I).
rulings.note: Rubric-caused tension: IVab's listing of realtors/estate agents pulls one way, rule 2's profession-on-own-account carve-out the other; the string does not state credentials.

rulings.rationale: Sunderland Polytechnic was a degree-granting higher-education institution; HE teaching professionals crosswalk to I (rule 8), not the school-teacher line in II.
A biochemist is a life-science professional (crosswalks to I); the health-associate-professional line in rule 8 covers technologists and technicians, not scientists.
Director General = head of an autonomous national trade association; string gives no evidence it is tiny, so rule 1's default applies, as with occ2_2512.
rulings.note: Rubric-caused split: same 'evidently tiny' burden-of-proof gap as occ2_2512; ruled identically for consistency.

rulings.rationale: Chairman of the family business = family proprietor; rule 2 sends ownership to IVab unless the firm is clearly large, which the string does not establish.

Lord Chancellor is a cabinet office held as a politician; the political role exhausts the string (rule 6). Hailsham's barrister career is real but not in the string, and coding it would import outside knowledge the rubric does not license.
Rule 6 skips the political first item (press secretary); the next substantive occupation is management consultancy, and rule 8 codes business professionals, including management consultants, as I.
A management trainee is not yet a manager — rule 1's II requires actual managerial or administrative duty; a trainee on rotational/routine work at that stated grade is routine non-manual.
rulings.note: Rubric-caused split: rule 5 codes careers 'at stated level' but says nothing about trainee grades, and management-trainee is a track, not a profession.

rulings.rationale: Single career in the family firm coded at stated level (MD) per rule 5; an MD of the family business is a proprietor-director, and rule 2 gives IVab absent clear evidence of large scale. Consistent with occ2_2522 and occ2_2690.
Chair of CND is typically an elected voluntary/honorific position and 'work with Shelter charity' states no occupation; no employment relation is established anywhere in the string (rule 7).

The dates show a chronological listing, defeating rule 5's premise that the first item is the principal role; the principal occupation is the 8-year lectureship, coded II absent university-faculty evidence (teacher line).
rulings.note: Rubric-caused split: rule 5's first-listed heuristic assumes principal-first ordering; it misfires on explicitly dated chronological strings, coding a 2-year youth clerk job as class origin.

rulings.rationale: The string states own-account property development with no scale evidence; rule 2's default is IVab unless the firm is clearly large, and the rubric does not license using biographical knowledge of the named individual to establish scale.
rulings.note: Rubric gap: whether a parenthetical naming a specific well-known person admits external evidence of scale is undefined; A and B split exactly on that.

rulings.rationale: Trainee solicitor at a major firm is inside the credentialled legal profession's formal track, performing legal work; crosswalk practice codes trainees to the profession trained for → legal professional, I. Political assistant item is skipped under rule 6.
rulings.note: Rubric-caused split: rubric is silent on professionals-in-training.

rulings.rationale: One ascending social-care career (care worker → officer in charge → project director → national director); rule 5 forbids selecting between grades within a career and codes at stated level — national director of a small charity is lower service, II.
rulings.note: Rule 5's career-vs-list boundary is the crux: multiple employers made B read it as separate occupations.

rulings.rationale: Commissioned officer, rank unstated; without evidence of senior rank, lower service class avoids inflation. Consistent with occ2_2554.
rulings.note: Rubric-caused split: no military line in the schema.

rulings.rationale: Captain is an explicitly junior/mid commissioned rank; lower service. Consistent with the convention applied to occ2_2554 and occ2_2884.
rulings.note: Rubric-caused split: no military line in the schema.

rulings.rationale: First-listed: CIA analyst. Intelligence/policy analysts crosswalk to administration professionals (rule 8) → I; 'analyst' is a graded professional occupation, not a seniority claim needing scale evidence.

First-listed: Air Force pilot. Both crosswalk routes converge on II — a pilot maps to aircraft-pilot associate professional, and a junior/unranked commissioned officer codes lower service under the convention applied to the other military items.
rulings.note: Rubric-caused split: no military line in the schema.

rulings.rationale: Face value of 'labor union president (SEIU)' is head of the named large union; rule 1's default codes the head of a large organisation I absent evidence of a tiny unit.
rulings.note: Rubric-caused split: string cannot distinguish national from local presidency; rule 1's burden-of-proof direction, not the string, decides.

rulings.rationale: 'Financial administrator' is indeterminate between clerical (III) and lower administrator (II), and the remaining jobs (manual labourer, sports reporter) span classes without clarifying the first; rule 7 prefers missing to a silent coin-flip.
A Reserve commission is a part-time role, not the substantive occupation; the substantive occupation is owner of a media group, and rule 2 gives IVab absent clear evidence of large scale.

'Lecturer' with no institution named: I requires evidence of a degree-granting HE post; without it the teacher line in II is the non-inflating reading. Press secretary (political) is second-listed and skipped. Consistent with occ2_2785; contrast occ2_2590/occ2_2673 where the institution is stated.

Journalist is named in II; deputy editor, bureau chief and editor-at-large are senior grades within journalism, not organisational headship, so rule 5's within-career stated-level clause does not lift it to I.
Instructor at Camosun College — a community college, largely sub-degree/vocational teaching — sits on the teacher/vocational-instructor line in II, unlike degree-granting HE (occ2_2673).
First-listed substantive occupation is architect, a credentialled professional (I); city councillor is political and journalist is second-listed.

Rule 6 skips the legislative assistant; 'law clerk' with no court or firm named is indeterminate between a judicial clerkship (professional entry, I-track) and clerical legal support (III). Both coders were at low confidence; rule 7 says code unknown.

Texas JP is an elected office and it exhausts the string; rule 6's stated principle is that an elected role is not a class origin, and Texas JPs need not hold any prior legal occupation the string could reveal.
rulings.note: Rubric ambiguity: rule 6's examples are legislative/executive; a salaried elected judicial office is arguably an occupation, which is exactly where A and B split.

rulings.rationale: Chief of staff and campaign manager are political staff roles; executive director of EMILY's List, a PAC, is employment inside a purely electoral-political organisation. Political roles exhaust the string (rule 6).
rulings.note: Rubric ambiguity: whether paid leadership of a PAC/advocacy organisation counts as a 'political role' or a managerial occupation is undefined.

rulings.rationale: VP of marketing is a functional director, not head of the firm; rule 1's worked rule codes functional directors II even in a large company.
rulings.note: Rubric-caused split: class I's 'managers of large organisations' clause conflicts with the worked rule's 'functional directors are II'; the worked rule is the operative tiebreaker.

rulings.rationale: President of a denominational conference center is head of a single facility owned by a parent body, not of an autonomous firm; scale and autonomy are not evident, so lower service (rule 1).

CSQ is a large Quebec union central; its president is head of a large workers' organisation, a higher administrator under rule 1. Consistent with occ2_2964's face-value treatment of named-union presidencies.
rulings.note: Same local-vs-national ambiguity as occ2_2964; rule 1's default direction decides.

rulings.rationale: 'Career military officer', rank unspecified. By analogy with rule 1 (no evidence of seniority/scale defaults to the lower service class), an officer of unstated rank codes II; field-grade colonel+ would be I.
rulings.note: Rubric gap: the schema is silent on commissioned officers and rule 8's crosswalk direction for the military is contested — the split is rubric-caused. Same policy applied to 0340, 0696, 0720, 0977.

rulings.rationale: 'Reporter, then publisher/editor' is an explicit within-career progression, and rule 5 codes a single career at its stated level, not entry grade. Publisher of the Dothan Eagle is head of an actual firm, not evidently tiny (rule 1), so I.

'Managed family businesses incl. amusement park' — modal reading is a member of the proprietor family running the family's own businesses, i.e. proprietor-manager (rule 2); no evidence of large scale.
Rule 6 strips the legislative chief-of-staff and the seat. Financial adviser at a bank matches ISCO-08 2412 financial and investment advisers — a finance professional, which rule 8 assigns to I.
rulings.note: Minor rubric gap: rule 8 does not draw the finance professional (2412) vs associate (3312) line; here the title matches the professional category.

rulings.rationale: Political staff stripped (rule 6); first substantive is OTB shift manager. The EGP schema places managers of small establishments and supervisors of non-manual employees in II, and rule 1's unspecified-manager default is II, not III.
rulings.note: Rubric-caused split: rule 1 never addresses first-line supervisors of routine service workers; resolved from the underlying schema, which puts non-manual supervisors in II.

rulings.rationale: Executive director is head of the organisation, not a functional director. A statewide medical association is not evidently tiny, so rule 1's worked rule (head of an actual organisation is I) applies.

Rule 2: ownership moves people to IV unless the firm is clearly large. The funeral home + burial-insurance + land/timber/gravel portfolio is the classic diversified small-town proprietor pattern; wealth is implied but no firm is stated to be large.

Scale, not title: the organisation (major coal company, Murray Energy successor) is evidently large, and the class definition places managers of large organisations in I. A VP is higher management, not a scale-unknown functional director.
rulings.note: Rubric-caused split: rule 1's categorical 'functional directors are II' collides with 'managers of large organisations' (I) when scale IS evident; ruled that the scale principle governs, since the functional-director clause exists to handle unknown scale.

rulings.rationale: The string names the individual (Tom Casten), who founded and ran Trigen Energy Corp, a large NYSE-listed firm — 'code the organisation implied'. Large proprietor/CEO, not petty bourgeoisie.
rulings.note: Rubric gap: nothing says whether external identification of a named person may establish scale; string alone would be unknown/IVab.

rulings.rationale: Lt Governor is elected (rule 6). The first substantive item is Delaware Secretary of Finance — a higher public administrator running a state finance department — which is I; the county Deputy CAO is consistent with senior administration.
rulings.note: Rubric-caused split: rule 6 lists ministerial staffers but is silent on appointed cabinet offices; ruled they are administration, not party politics.

rulings.rationale: 'County/state aid coordinator' spans clerical program coordination (III) and lower administration (II) with no modal reading and no credential or scope evidence; rule 7 — a coin flip between II and III should not enter the data as a class.

The string affirms he was a student when first elected — a known absence of any pre-political occupation, i.e. politics was the first career. That is rule 6's none-political case; unknown would misrecord known absence as missing data.
rulings.note: Rubric-caused split: the boundary between none-political (known absence) and unknown (missing data) is implicit in rules 6-7. Contrast 0542, ruled unknown.

rulings.rationale: First-listed 'insurance company worker': the non-professional insurance workforce is overwhelmingly routine office/sales staff, and bios name professional grades (underwriter, executive) when held — stated assumption, so III. Same modal logic as 0480.
Rule 8's consultant clause requires a named professional field; 'defense' names a sector, not a profession — the consultant could be a retired officer, engineer, or lobbyist. Unknown.
'Navy officer', rank unspecified; unspecified commissioned officer defaults to lower service II (policy per 0024); subsequent role is political staff.
rulings.note: Rubric gap on military officers — rubric-caused split.

rulings.rationale: Council seat stripped (rule 6). 'Senior policy advisor' to two UN Secretaries-General is a higher-grade professional post at the top of the international civil service; the explicit seniority marker places it in I.
rulings.note: Rule 8 is silent on policy professionals (see 0824/0865/0879); the seniority marker, absent there, decides here.

rulings.rationale: Role unstated over a 30-year postal career, but the modal postal occupations — clerk and letter carrier — both crosswalk to clerical/routine non-manual (ISCO 441x), so III on a stated assumption rather than unknown.

'UAW local secretary' underdetermines employment relations: local secretaries are typically lay officers employed as manufacturing workers (VIIab), but the string could denote a union official (II) — opposite sides of the schema, so rule 7.
rulings.note: Rubric-caused in part: rule 6 covers elected/party roles but not union offices, and rule 5 gives no way to decide whether the office or the implied underlying job is the occupation.

rulings.rationale: First-listed bare 'banker': modally a bank officer/manager; absent any seniority or scale evidence the rule-1 default is the lower service class, II, not I (which would require assuming executive or professional grade).

'Apollo program worker' is role-indeterminate with no modal class (engineers, technicians and assemblers all substantial), so it cannot be coded; the next codable item is real estate company founder — the rubric lists realtors/own-account proprietors under IVab, and no scale is stated (rule 2).
rulings.note: Rubric-caused: nothing says whether an uncodable first item yields to the next listed occupation; ruled that it does, by analogy with rule 6's skip. Same gap in 0747 and 0845.

rulings.rationale: Rules 2+8 together: a computing professional practising on his own account codes on the profession, not the proprietorship, and computing professionals are I. Co-founder of an IT consulting company is modally a practising IT consultant.

'No professional role explicitly stated' is the compiler flagging missing data, not an affirmed absence — an unrecorded broadcasting job between training and the 1975 election is entirely possible. Rule 7: unknown, unlike 0269 where student status at election affirms absence.
rulings.note: Same rule 6/7 boundary gap as 0269 — rubric-caused.

rulings.rationale: Erie City Controller is an elected office and chief of staff to a state senator is political staff; under rule 6's letter these exhaust the string with no substantive occupation remaining.
rulings.note: Rubric-caused: rule 6's list omits elected administrative offices (controller, sheriff); ruled by its general clause that an elected role is not a class origin, since unlike 0711 there is no underlying occupational career here.

rulings.rationale: Teacher-to-superintendent is the canonical single education career (superintendents are former teachers by requirement), so rule 5's within-career clause codes the stated top level; a district superintendent is a higher administrator heading a district — I.
rulings.note: Rubric-caused in part: rule 5 gives no standard for progression markers, and 'and' is weaker than the example's 'rising to'; ruled on the modal single-career reading.

rulings.rationale: Political items stripped (rule 6). The rubric itself puts 'professor' in I and (school) 'teacher' in II; college teaching sides with the higher-education professionals (ISCO 2310 to I in the standard crosswalk, which does not condition on rank). Consistent with 0691, 0694.

Mortgage banking is credit/loan origination — an associate finance occupation (ISCO 3312-type), not a 2412-type finance professional — and no seniority is stated, so II. Distinct from 0134's financial adviser, where the title matches the professional category.
B's code is missing, not a substantive disagreement. First-listed substantive is attorney (rule 5); mayoralty is political (rule 6); lawyer is I.

'Taught at the college level' is postsecondary teaching; the rubric places professor in I and the crosswalk maps higher-education teaching to I regardless of stated rank. Consistent with 0622 and 0694.
'Educator, Edward Waters University' is university teaching staff — higher-education professional, I per the crosswalk and the rubric's placement of professor in I; legislature stripped (rule 6).
First-listed substantive is Army field artillery officer (the later prosecutorial career is second-listed, rule 5); rank unspecified, so lower service II per the military policy applied at 0024.
rulings.note: Rubric gap on military officers — rubric-caused split.

rulings.rationale: Deputy-then-sheriff over 41 years is exactly rule 5's worked example — one police career coded at its stated level, not entry grade. Head of the Jacksonville Sheriff's Office, a major metropolitan force, is a higher administrator: I.
rulings.note: Rubric-caused: rule 5's within-career clause and rule 6's stripping of elected office directly conflict when the career tops out in an elected post; ruled that a 41-year occupational career is not a political class origin.

rulings.rationale: Navy pilot is a commissioned officer; nine years' active duty implies junior/mid rank (lieutenant to lieutenant commander), so lower service II per the military policy; later items are political staff (rule 6).
rulings.note: Rubric gap on military officers — rubric-caused split.

rulings.rationale: President of the family-owned Smucker Company is modally a member of the owning family, and rule 2 makes ownership dominate: IVab unless the firm is clearly large, which a scale-unstated commercial construction firm is not.
rulings.note: Rubric-caused: rule 1 (head of actual firm defaults to I) and rule 2 (owner defaults to IVab) give opposite defaults for owner-heads of mid-scale firms; ruled that the ownership rule, which explicitly contemplates this case ('owned and operated a trucking company'), governs.

rulings.rationale: 'State Department and USAID staff' states no grade and is uncodable; the next codable substantive occupation is attorney at White & Case — lawyer, I. Skipping an uncodable item is not the highest-position cherry-picking rule 5 forbids.
rulings.note: Same rubric gap as 0503: the rubric is silent on whether an uncodable first item yields to the next listed occupation — rubric-caused split.

rulings.rationale: First-listed is CIA analyst (rule 5 bars reaching the second-listed U.S. Attorney). An analyst with no seniority marker codes as lower-service professional grade, II — consistent with 0865/0879, with 'senior' promoting to I as in 0407.
rulings.note: Rubric-caused: rule 8 names business, finance and computing professionals as I but is silent on policy/intelligence analysts; adjudicated by the schema's grade logic.

rulings.rationale: Context resolves 'engineer' to the operating side, and rule 4 explicitly assigns operating engineers to V/VI; 'driller/engineer' reads as a skilled oilfield operator rather than an unskilled labourer.
rulings.note: Rubric-caused tension: 'driller' parallels the VIIab exemplar 'miner' while rule 4 puts operating engineers in V/VI; ruled on rule 4's explicit assignment. The two readings are adjacent manual classes.

rulings.rationale: 'Financial services (Citi Financial)' names an industry with no role and is uncodable; the next codable item, university athletic development official, is a lower administrator — II.
rulings.note: Same uncodable-first-item gap as 0503/0747 — rubric-caused split.

rulings.rationale: First-listed conflict analyst for an NGO: analyst with no seniority or managerial marker codes lower-service II per the analyst policy (0824, 0879).
rulings.note: Rule 8's silence on policy analysts is the underlying rubric gap.

rulings.rationale: First-listed policy analyst at the Department of Labor, no seniority marker: II. Rule 5 bars promoting on the later law-firm partnership, and the Senate counsel post is political staff (rule 6).
rulings.note: Rule 8's silence on policy analysts is the underlying rubric gap — rubric-caused split.

rulings.rationale: B's code is missing, not a substantive disagreement. Rank is stated: Navy lieutenant, a junior commissioned officer — lower service II, consistent with the military policy applied at 0024.
rulings.note: Military-officer mapping is a rubric gap, though the stated junior rank makes II the clear side of it.

rulings.rationale: 'Ohio BMV employee' is employment, not a substantive occupation; rule 5's word 'substantive' plus the rule 6 skip pattern licence moving to the first codable item, teaching English (II). The ruling is robust: every later item (safety director, program manager, small-company manager) is also II.
rulings.note: Rubric ambiguity: it never says whether a roleless first item ('X employee') is skipped or forces unknown. Resolved here by analogy to rule 6; state the skip rule explicitly.

rulings.rationale: Rule 6 skips the aide roles. 'SBA senior post' is an administrative post at a federal agency, so the range is III-I, and 'senior' excludes III; rule 1's default for managers of unspecified grade is II, not I. B's I needs evidence of higher-administrator grade the string does not give.

First-listed substantive occupation is 'Air Force officer' (rule 5); rank unstated. Applying rule 1's unspecified-grade default within the service classes, an officer of unstated rank codes II; junior commissioned ranks are also modal.
rulings.note: Rubric ambiguity, recurring: the rubric is silent on commissioned officers of unstated rank, and coders split I/II randomly (both coders took each side across cases). It needs an explicit default; II applied uniformly here.

rulings.rationale: 'Worked for Columbia Gas' is roleless and skipped as non-substantive; first codable item is 'family farm/general store', which implies operating the holding. Rule 3's default (farm without role marker -> IVc, medium) applies; farm is listed before the store.
rulings.note: Same roleless-first-item gap as occ2_0981.

rulings.rationale: Naval aviator is a commissioned flying officer; both the officer default (see occ2_1008) and the pilot crosswalk (aircraft pilots are associate professionals -> II) agree on II.
rulings.note: Officer-rank rubric gap, as in occ2_1008.

rulings.rationale: First-listed 'Air Force officer', rank unstated -> II per the uniform officer ruling. Mayor is political (rule 6); ROTC assistant professorship is a later item under rule 5.
rulings.note: Officer-rank rubric gap, as in occ2_1008.

rulings.rationale: Nurse's aide is personal-care service work (ISCO 5132), which is IIIb and stays with III in this seven-class collapse; the rubric's III explicitly includes 'service', while its VIIab exemplars are labourer/cleaner/factory work.
rulings.note: Rubric ambiguity: the IIIb-vs-VIIab treatment of unqualified care work is not stated; some EGP collapses move IIIb to VII. Ruled III per the rubric's own class III wording; worth an explicit line.

rulings.rationale: None-political fails: 'special prosecutor's office staff' and 'DOJ special assistant' are government legal employment, not elected or party roles, so political items do not exhaust the string. But 'staff' carries no grade (attorney vs clerk), so rule 7 controls.
rulings.note: Partly rubric-caused: rule 6's boundary for appointive government staff (vs elected/party roles) is undefined.

rulings.rationale: First-listed military officer, rank unstated -> II per the uniform officer ruling; the physician career is second-listed (rule 5).
rulings.note: Officer-rank rubric gap, as in occ2_1008.

rulings.rationale: A novitiate is pre-ordination training, not clergy employment, so II cannot be anchored; 'insurance industry (community outreach)' names a field and a function but no grade (III-II span). Rule 7: both items underdetermine.
First-listed 'Navy officer', rank unstated -> II per the uniform officer ruling; the Kirkland & Ellis attorney career is second-listed and rule 5 forbids taking it.
rulings.note: Officer-rank rubric gap, as in occ2_1008.

rulings.rationale: 'Nonprofit/education practice director' at a law firm names a practice area, and practice-area leadership in a law firm is a senior-lawyer (partner-level) role; non-lawyer directors carry functional titles (marketing, HR), not practice names. Rule 2's spirit: code the profession at its stated senior level.

Dean of students manages one function of the university, not the institution; rule 1's worked rule assigns functional directors within an organisation to II regardless of the organisation's size. Notre Dame's scale describes the university, not the post's headship.
rulings.note: Rubric-caused: class I's bare 'higher administrators' invites A's reading; the worked rule's functional-director branch decides it, but the tension is in the rubric.

rulings.rationale: 'Business and finance' names a field with no role and is skipped as non-substantive; first codable occupation is pastor -> clergy, II.
rulings.note: Same roleless-first-item gap as occ2_0981; A rightly flagged it.

rulings.rationale: 'Alcoholics Recovery Project worker' is first-listed (rule 5) and 'worker' carries no qualification or grade marker: qualified social worker (II) and unqualified support worker (III) are both live, and the later welfare-sector items do not fix the first item's grade. Rule 7.
Elected NUS/Scottish NUS presidencies are elected offices, and the only other item is party staff; under rule 6 the string is exhausted by elected and party roles, leaving no market occupation.
rulings.note: Rubric-caused: rule 6's list does not say whether elected association/union offices count as political roles or as association-official occupations (II). Ruled on rule 6's stated principle that an elected role is not a class origin.

rulings.rationale: First-listed principal occupation is bare 'civil servant', which spans clerical III to senior administrator I (rule 7); 'formerly electrician' is a prior occupation rule 5 forbids taking, and using it to infer a clerical grade is a contextual guess.
rulings.note: Rubric ambiguity, recurring: no default grade for bare civil servant / government officer (cf. occ2_1517, 1582, 1642, 1771). If the analysis needs these, the rubric should state a modal-grade default like rule 3's for farmers.

rulings.rationale: AM staff and party employment are political (rule 6); the remaining item, 'Citizens Advice Cymru worker', gives no role or grade (adviser, administrator, manager all possible). Rule 7.

The rubric explicitly lists 'brokers' under IVab; rule 8's crosswalk applies only where the rubric is silent, and it is not. Historically stockbrokers were exchange members trading on commission, matching IVab's commission-agent logic.
rulings.note: Rubric could clarify precedence of explicit class exemplars over rule 8, but the text as written decides for IVab.

rulings.rationale: Councillor skipped (rule 6); UDR/TA soldier is a uniformed other-rank. The rubric's nearest anchor is police and fire other-ranks, which it places in V/VI; soldiers are assimilated to that anchor.
rulings.note: Rubric-caused: soldiers' other ranks are unlisted, and coders split V/VI vs VIIab in mirror-image across the two soldier cases. Ruled V/VI both times by the police/fire anchor; the rubric should name the class for other-ranks service personnel.

rulings.rationale: First-listed 'Local Government Officer' is a substantive occupation of unstated grade spanning clerical to chief officer; rule 5 blocks the codable BBC role, and rule 7 blocks guessing the LGO grade.
rulings.note: Recurring bare-officer gap; see occ2_1472.

rulings.rationale: 'Newspaper editor' denotes the editor of a newspaper, i.e. head of its editorial organisation; rule 1 puts the head of an actual organisation in I unless evidently tiny, and the life peerage corroborates a national-scale figure rather than a parish weekly. The peerage itself is not coded.

Optometrist is a degree-qualified, registered practitioner; ISCO-08 classifies optometrists at 2267 among health professionals with dentists and pharmacists, mapping to I. Rule 8's II examples (paramedics, health technologists) name associate-grade credentials and do not cover optometrists.
rulings.note: Rubric-caused: 'standard ISCO-to-EGP mappings' is unversioned — ISCO-88 (3224, associate -> II) and ISCO-08 (2267, professional -> I) disagree exactly here. Ruled on the current standard; the rubric should pin a version.

rulings.rationale: Bare 'company director (Castlemead Ltd)' fits neither rule 1 branch: headship (managing director) is not established, so I is not licensed, and it is not a functional director, so the II residual does not cleanly fire; a proprietor-director (IVab) reading is also live. Three defensible classes -> unknown.
rulings.note: Rubric-caused: rule 1 has no branch for a bare non-functional 'company director' of a named firm, a common UK formula that spans I/II/IVab.

rulings.rationale: Co-founder of a firm is a proprietor; rule 2 sends proprietors to IVab 'unless the firm is clearly large', and the string states no scale. B's I imports external knowledge of Osborne & Little's later prominence, and at founding it was small.
rulings.note: Rubric-caused in part: whether external knowledge of a named firm's scale is admissible is unstated. Ruled on the string per rule 2's default.

rulings.rationale: 'Sales/marketing at Ford' spans sales representative (III) to marketing executive (I) with no level given, and the second item is likewise a field without a role. Rule 7's exemplar is directly on point; B's associate-professional reading is a guess.
First-listed bare 'council officer' spans clerical to senior administrator with no grade marker; rule 5 blocks the second item and rule 7 blocks the modal guess.
rulings.note: Recurring bare-officer gap; see occ2_1472.

rulings.rationale: First-listed paratrooper is a uniformed other-rank; assimilated to the rubric's police/fire other-ranks anchor in V/VI, consistent with occ2_1514.
rulings.note: Same soldier gap as occ2_1514 — the coders took opposite sides in the two cases, confirming the rubric, not the strings, caused the splits.

rulings.rationale: 'Worked at Sainsbury's' names an employer only; the role spans shelf-stacker (VIIab) through checkout (III) to store manager (II). Rule 7: no role, no code.
'Foreign and Commonwealth Office official' spans registry clerk to senior diplomat; 'official' is not a grade. Rule 7 over B's assumption that official denotes administrative rank.
rulings.note: Recurring bare-officer/official gap; see occ2_1472.

rulings.rationale: First-listed 'British Army officer', rank unstated -> II per the uniform officer ruling; 'banking' is a later, roleless item anyway.
rulings.note: Officer-rank rubric gap, as in occ2_1008.

rulings.rationale: Rule 4: bare 'engineer'. The merchant-navy context does not disambiguate — it is compatible with a certificated marine engineer officer (II), a skilled engine-room artificer (V/VI), or a rating (VIIab) — and NUPE membership pulls yet another way. Context that points three ways is not context enough.

A research officer at a plant-breeding research institute is a graduate scientist grade; scientists crosswalk to I (rule 8), and a junior grade within a profession does not demote the profession to II, just as a junior doctor is still I.

Teacher and head teacher are grades within one education career, so rule 5's career clause codes the career at its stated level: founding head of Highbury Grove, a large London comprehensive. Head of an actual, not-tiny organisation -> I (rule 1).

First-listed scientific laboratory assistant does bench work in the technician family; the rubric's non-supervisory technicians sit in V/VI, and class III's exemplars (clerical, secretarial, sales, service) fit worse. 'Assistant' marks a junior grade, not a different class family.
rulings.note: Rubric-caused at the margin: assistant-grade lab work is placed nowhere explicitly; III remains defensible.

rulings.rationale: The three items are separately listed occupations at different firms, not grades within one listed item, so rule 5's career clause ('rising to' phrasing) does not textually apply; first-listed is head of client services at a small software firm — a functional manager, II under rule 1.
rulings.note: Rubric-caused: rule 5's premise (first = principal/most recent) visibly fails on this chronologically ascending string ending at Lehman chief architect (I), and the career-clause boundary for same-field jobs across employers is undefined. Ruled on rule 5's letter; the rubric should address ascending-order strings.

rulings.rationale: First-listed bare 'local government officer' spans clerical to chief officer; rule 5 blocks master mariner (second-listed) and rule 7 blocks guessing the grade.
rulings.note: Recurring bare-officer gap; see occ2_1472.

rulings.rationale: First-listed care worker (rule 5; the physiotherapist reading would take the second occupation) is personal-care service work -> IIIb -> III in this collapse, consistent with occ2_1098.
rulings.note: Same IIIb/VIIab care-work gap as occ2_1098.

rulings.rationale: 'RAF officer', rank unstated -> II per the uniform officer ruling.
rulings.note: Officer-rank rubric gap, as in occ2_1008.

rulings.rationale: 'Marketing and communications' is a field with no role or grade; the Blue Arrow board seat is an office held alongside that career, quite possibly non-executive, and unlike pastor or teacher it is not itself an occupation to skip to; the council seat is political. Rule 7: the principal occupation's grade is unstated.
rulings.note: Rubric-caused at the margin: whether a plc board directorship counts as a codable occupation (I) or a non-occupational office is unstated.
